design.title: Two-member committee: two independently trained localizers must agree before a fix is trusted; confidence is the smaller of the two members' belief on the consensus block
design.eli5: Instead of one navigator the drone now carries two, trained separately on the same three photographs of Berlin: each starts from a different random state and sees every training picture under its own random lighting and blur, so each picks up its own habits and blind spots. When a brand-new photograph fools a navigator, it tends to fool each one differently, so they point at different places; the drone then says 'not sure' and waits for the next frame instead of flying on a wrong fix. Only when both navigators point at the same place does the drone accept it. It is the same reason you ask two witnesses separately: two independent accounts that agree are worth far more than one confident voice.
design.hypothesis: The stage no experiment in this era has questioned is the confidence gate, and it is where the score is being lost. On the held-out 2024 photograph the false-fix rate has sat at 39-43% through three different training designs (exp 4: 38.75%, exp 5: 42.25%, exp 6: 43.0%) while usable sat at 12-14%; false fixes cost three times what usable fixes earn, and converting a false fix into an abstention is worth exactly as much to the mission score as finding a new usable fix. The single model's confidence is the pooled softmax mass of one classifier trained only on photographs it has memorised, so on a photograph it has not seen it is uninformative by construction: the founding measurement showed the 0.040 champion 97% confident while wrong, with 390 confident predictions on a foreign photograph collapsing onto 40 cells. That is the signature of a model that, given a foreign input, slides into whichever survey-specific shortcut the input happens to trigger. A different model, trained from a different random start on differently drawn augmentations, has different shortcuts and slides into different cells for the same foreign frame, while on frames where the shared street-and-building geometry genuinely names the cell both models land on the same block. Disagreement between independently trained models is the one uncertainty estimator the literature finds robust under dataset shift (deep ensembles, Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017; Ovadia et al. 2019 measured it dominating every learned or post-hoc calibrated single-model confidence as shift grows): it is epistemic uncertainty, which is what a never-seen survey produces, not aleatoric. The library (L2) lists learned aleatoric confidence as what does NOT transfer under map change, and the earlier eras' two honesty attempts were exactly that kind: four-area exp 15 (a field-shape confidence head) and exp 32 (abstention thresholds calibrated on never-trained blocks) re-score at 1.85 and 1.77 on this ruler, 85% and 77% false fix. No era has tried an ensemble (nothing in lineage_history mentions one). This is also materially different from the decode-time consensus the Prignitz detour refuted: that averaged ONE model's belief over four rotations of the same frame, and a wrong answer that is rotation-stable survives it; here two separately trained models are asked the same question, and a wrong answer must be shared by both to survive. Cost, measured at design time without training (runs/_probe_exp7_committee.py): two members with trunk widths [3,24,48,96,112] export to 3,942,411 bytes (3.76 MiB, under the 4 MiB gate) at 1.97 ms host latency, 971,864 parameters, versus the single 160-wide model's 3,080,677 bytes and 1.49 ms. Each member is narrower than today's single model (head 112x2970 = 333k vs 475k), so per-member fit on the training photographs will be somewhat lower; the committee's averaged belief is expected to recover most of it. The design is honest about what it targets: it attacks the false-fix term, not the usable term, and it is the gate every later accuracy experiment will also need.
